title: Naaman's Healing
overview: 2 Kings Chapter 5 recounts the miraculous healing of Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, who suffered from leprosy. The chapter highlights God's power to heal and deliver through the prophet Elisha, emphasizing faith, humility, and obedience. Naaman's initial pride and anger give way to repentance and acknowledgment of the God of Israel as the one true God. The chapter also contrasts the faithfulness of Elisha with the greed and deceit of his servant Gehazi, who suffers a curse as a result. This narrative demonstrates God's sovereignty over nations and individuals, His mercy extended even to Gentiles, and the importance of trusting God's instructions even when they seem simple or unexpected.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: Introduction of Naaman and the Captive Maid.** The chapter opens by introducing Naaman, a respected Syrian commander afflicted with leprosy, and the Israelite maid who suggests he seek healing from the prophet in Samaria. 

**Verses 6-8: The King's Reaction and Elisha's Intervention.** Naaman brings a letter from the Syrian king to the king of Israel, who reacts in despair, but Elisha reassures the king and invites Naaman to come to him.

**Verses 9-14: Naaman's Healing Process.** Elisha instructs Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan River. Naaman initially resists but eventually obeys and is healed.

**Verses 15-19: Naaman's Gratitude and Commitment.** Naaman acknowledges the God of Israel and offers gifts, which Elisha refuses. Naaman requests permission to worship only the LORD despite his political obligations.

**Verses 20-27: Gehazi's Greed and Punishment.** Gehazi deceitfully pursues Naaman to obtain gifts, resulting in Elisha pronouncing a leprous curse upon him, which is immediately fulfilled.

keyVerses.text: Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
keyVerses.significance: This verse captures the moment of Naaman's miraculous healing, emphasizing obedience to God's word through Elisha. It highlights the power of faith and God's ability to restore even the most hopeless conditions.

keyVerses.text: And he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him: and he said, Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel: now therefore, I pray thee, take a blessing of thy servant.
keyVerses.significance: Naaman's confession acknowledges the exclusive sovereignty of the God of Israel, marking a significant moment of faith and recognition of God's supremacy over all nations.

keyVerses.text: The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the consequence of Gehazi's greed and deceit, illustrating the holiness of God's servants and the severe judgment against sin, especially hypocrisy and dishonesty.

keyVerses.text: And Elisha sent a messenger unto him, saying, Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.
keyVerses.significance: Elisha's simple instruction tests Naaman's faith and humility, showing that God's healing often requires obedience to His word, even when it seems mundane or beneath one's dignity.

characters.name: Naaman
characters.description: Commander of the Syrian army, a mighty and honorable man afflicted with leprosy. His journey from pride and anger to faith and humility exemplifies God's power to heal and transform even Gentiles.

characters.name: Elisha
characters.description: The prophet of God in Israel who performs the miracle of healing Naaman. He represents God's authority and power, refusing gifts and demonstrating integrity and obedience to God's will.

characters.name: Gehazi
characters.description: Elisha's servant who greedily pursues Naaman for gifts after the healing. His deceit results in a divine curse of leprosy, serving as a warning against greed and dishonesty among God's servants.

characters.name: The Israelite Maid
characters.description: A captive servant in Naaman's household who first suggests that Naaman seek healing from the prophet in Israel, initiating the events of the chapter.

characters.name: God
characters.description: The sovereign Lord who grants healing and delivers through His prophet Elisha. He demonstrates mercy to a foreigner and enforces holiness through judgment on Gehazi.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes God's power to heal physical ailments as a sign of His mercy, extending even to Gentiles like Naaman, showing God's universal sovereignty and compassion.
Naaman's healing requires humble obedience to Elisha's instructions, illustrating that faith often involves trusting God's word even when it challenges human pride or expectations.
The narrative shows God's control over foreign kings and armies, affirming that He is the true God above all earthly powers and that His purposes extend beyond Israel.
Gehazi's punishment for greed highlights God's holiness and intolerance of sin, especially among those who serve Him, reinforcing the call to integrity and faithfulness.

historicalContext: This chapter is set during the 9th century BC in the period of the divided monarchy after Israel split from Judah. Syria (Aram) was a significant regional power often in conflict with Israel. Leprosy was a feared and socially isolating disease, considered both a physical and ceremonial impurity under Mosaic Law. Healing from leprosy was seen as a divine act. The political context involves the king of Syria sending Naaman to Israel, reflecting diplomatic relations and the recognition of Israel's prophetic authority. The Jordan River, where Naaman is healed, was a central geographic and symbolic location for Israel, representing purification and covenant identity.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God's sovereign grace in healing Naaman, highlighting that salvation and blessing come by faith and not by works or human merit. Gehazi's punishment underscores the holiness required of God's servants.

Dispensationalists see this chapter as illustrating God's unfolding plan to bless the Gentiles through Israel. Naaman’s healing prefigures the inclusion of Gentiles in the covenant blessings, foreshadowing the New Testament gospel.

Early church interpreters often viewed Naaman's healing as a type of baptism, with the Jordan River symbolizing cleansing from sin. Gehazi’s leprosy is seen as a warning against greed and hypocrisy within the church.

crossReferences.connection: Jesus heals ten lepers, and only one returns to give thanks, paralleling Naaman’s healing and his grateful response.
The suffering servant bears our infirmities and diseases, connecting to God’s power to heal physical and spiritual afflictions as seen in Naaman’s story.
Peter’s declaration that God shows no partiality echoes the chapter’s theme of God’s mercy extending to Gentiles like Naaman.
The psalmist praises God for forgiving sins and healing diseases, reflecting the healing miracle in 2 Kings 5.
God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, a principle demonstrated by Naaman’s initial pride and eventual humility.

application: Trust God’s instructions even when they seem simple or beneath your expectations, as obedience leads to blessing.
Recognize God’s sovereignty over all nations and circumstances, encouraging prayer for leaders and those in authority.
Practice humility by submitting to God’s word and timing, especially in difficult trials or healing.
Guard against greed and dishonesty, especially in ministry or service to God, remembering Gehazi’s example.
Express gratitude to God for His blessings and deliverance, following Naaman’s example of returning to thank Elisha.
conclusion: 2 Kings 5 powerfully illustrates God’s sovereign ability to heal and transform lives through faith and obedience. Naaman’s story challenges believers to trust God’s word humbly, regardless of personal pride or cultural expectations. The chapter also warns against greed and unfaithfulness through Gehazi’s downfall, underscoring the holiness required of those who serve God. Ultimately, it reveals God’s mercy extending beyond Israel to the Gentiles, affirming His universal lordship and the call for all to acknowledge Him as the one true God.
timeline: c. 9th century BC - Period of the Divided Monarchy during the reign of the kings of Israel and Syria

outline.heading: Naaman and the Captive Maid
outline.description: Introduction of Naaman’s leprosy and the Israelite maid’s suggestion to seek healing from the prophet in Israel, setting the stage for God’s intervention.

outline.heading: The King of Israel’s Distress and Elisha’s Assurance
outline.description: The king of Israel reacts with despair to the Syrian king’s letter, but Elisha reassures him and invites Naaman to come for healing.

outline.heading: Naaman’s Healing by Obedience
outline.description: Naaman initially resists but ultimately obeys Elisha’s command to wash in the Jordan seven times, resulting in his complete healing.

outline.heading: Naaman’s Gratitude and Profession of Faith
outline.description: Naaman acknowledges the God of Israel as the only true God and offers gifts, which Elisha refuses, while Naaman commits to worshiping the LORD alone.

outline.heading: Gehazi’s Greed and Punishment
outline.description: Elisha’s servant Gehazi deceitfully obtains gifts from Naaman and is struck with leprosy as divine judgment for his greed and dishonesty.
